content:
Recently, there have been a number of large scale formalisation projects in maths and physics heavily using AIs like chatGPT and Claude (similar to: https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.03298 but for Lean). Some of these have been led by experts and others by relative outsiders.

I'm interested in the fairly broad question about when these formalisations can be considered useful, to whom and why and more generally when as a community we should embracing them and when should be discarding them.

For example: Do we think that these large-scale AI projects help in producing mathlib ready code? Do they help the authors themselves? Do they help others? etc.

I understand that some of these are very context-dependent, but I think they are important questions. I'm hoping that by answering some of them we might be able to shine a light on AI formalisations for new members of the community who join with this in mind.

For a start: I have always believed that Math Inc's recent announcements about sphere packing are very hollow. Sure, the AI system delivered a sorry-free proof, but all the auxiliary definitions and theorems thus generated are – by themselves – there only because the proof needs them. There is a lot of material that is more generally useful, but AI can never give an indication as to where it is in its output.

By contrast, the entirely human-driven Carleson project (which I worked on intensely in 2024 and 2025, and which basically led to me getting into my current PhD programme) found some gaps in the way mathlib expressed integrals, measures and other objects. These gaps were patched as the project went on, i.e. mathlib and Carleson improved each other.

In short, AI autoformalisation of proofs can only be useful if in the process it indicates a generally applicable theory of something that mathlib lacks, and it expresses that theory in a form that mathlib could "digest". Going straight for the big theorems using AI is like building a private library – it benefits far less people than it would if it were public.

It is also perfectly conceivable that two different AI systems could produce two different formalisations of one pen-and-paper definition (e.g. the Carlson symmetric form of elliptic integrals, or even combinatorial embeddings). Which one is better? Could both be improved on? These cannot be resolved by AI alone; humans would need to compare. Otherwise the towers built on these definitions would not be interoperable.

Jeremy Tan said:

In short, AI autoformalisation of proofs can only be useful if in the process it indicates a generally applicable theory of something that mathlib lacks, and it expresses that theory in a form that mathlib could "digest". Going straight for the big theorems using AI is like building a private library – it benefits far less people than it would if it were public.

I would be interested in whether people think it really is as bad as a private library, or whether having a formalisation no matter how bad or specific is still helpful independent of how it is generated?

I was thinking that maybe if the output itself is not useful - use can still be gotten from the workflow that lead to that output if that is described. But I'm not sure what the point is of knowing a great workflow that produces a non useful output, so I think the question still pivots to the use of the output (could be wrong here though)

I think that there are multiple reasons for wanting a formalization, and an AI tool might currently tick some but not all of those boxes.

Example: an AI formalization today of a proof of FLT would tick very few boxes, because everyone knows the theorem is true, it is of no use to anyone (it doesn't have any applications) and three of the main motivations of the development as far as I am concerned: (1) to get a human-readable clean modern proof written down (2) to isolate good abstractions and (3) to formalize important definitions used in the proof and get them into mathlib, might well not have been attained.

Example: an AI formalization today of the proof of the classification of finite simple groups would definitely be of value, because the length of the proof (14 volumes) and the fact that it is still not properly published (although it will be soon, hopefully) have raised doubts in people's minds in the community about the correctness of the result, and a huge number of other results in finite group theory and beyond rest on this important classification theorem.

Example: an AI formalization today of Mochizuki's proof of the ABC conjecture would have extreme positive value and would leave the mathematics community with a huge amount of egg on its face. One might argue that this is unlikely to happen, however an attempted AI formalization which isolated a concrete issue which Mochizuki then confessed to be a problem with his work would also definitely be a net positive value.

I think the FLT example is interesting, because it is an example of a topic A which there is an ongoing human effort to formalize, people in the community care about, and likely care about doing it right. So let's say Math Inc or some other company or group comes along and auto-formalizes FLT or a similar topic A, which is known to be true, in the same style as AI-autoformalizations today, is this a net-positivity for the community (it no doubt is for the company), a net-zero (i.e. it doesn't matter) or a net-negative?

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

Is this a net-positivity for the community (it no doubt is for the company), a net-zero (i.e. it doesn't matter) or a net-negative?

A more complex theorem proved by an autoformaliser (i.e. top-down) means more human follow-up work has to be done to extract the generally useful theories proved along the way. That takes time that could be better spent simply developing those useful theories from the ground up.

In short: the bigger the theorem the more net negative its monolithic autoformalisation becomes to the wider community. Smaller, immediately reusable autoformalisations are still net positive.

As an example, I wrote the initial version of docs#Polynomial.dvd_of_infinite_eval_dvd_eval with the help of Aristotle (#34845, #PR reviews > Jeremy Tan's open PRs @ 💬). It was not a very slick proof, and Buzzard and Gouëzel noticed this; my successive interactions with them (see #PR reviews > #34868 – more general polynomial asymptotics) generated many more useful lemmas for mathlib in #34868 and #34920, including lemmas not used in the slickened proof of the initial statement.

I recommend "pair programming" when working with autoformalisers:

  • You (the human) write some simple definitions
  • The AI proves basic theory about those definitions
  • You refactor the AI's output into something more usable and human-comprehensible
  • The AI proves some further theory (not a lot) using your refactored theorems
  • Repeat the last two steps

This should ensure that neither side gets too far ahead: you will neither be overwhelmed trying to distill the AI's output, nor lose yourself writing a long blueprint or other prompt that you hope the AI will follow.
I agree with Jeremy that right now it's time to work out how to use these tools or, to put it another way, how to collaborate with machines.

Example: an AI formalization today of Mochizuki's proof of the ABC conjecture would have extreme positive value and would leave the mathematics community with a huge amount of egg on its face. One might argue that this is unlikely to happen, however an attempted AI formalization which isolated a concrete issue which Mochizuki then confessed to be a problem with his work would also definitely be a net positive value.

Is "isolating a problem" – not just failing to prove something, but identifying a specific obstacle to why it doesn't work – something that current AI's are capable of doing? I gather some AI's automatically try to disprove as well as prove the given goal, and are very good at detecting minor misformalisations in statements in the process (starting sums at 0 instead of 1, that sort of thing); but if the AI can't find either a proof or a counterexample, can it give you a coherent account of where it got stuck, other than "I couldn't prove this lemma"? This is something that's also hard for humans!

To paraphrase a bit what I’ve seen here, and what I have gathered to some members of the AI side of the community. (I’m writing this to help myself with the framing of these projects).

It seems that there is an opinion that: these large-scale AI-formalizations do not currently produce code which is useful in producing Mathlib-ready code. I don’t think anyone actually claims otherwise (if they do please let me know). However, I think this is a requirement that some in the community (including myself) have a tendency to look towards when we are evaluating these projects (rightfully or wrongfully).

I’m focusing here on large-scale AI-formalizations. It has been acknowledged that there are likely other ways to use AI which may be useful for producing Mathlib ready-code, and that these are worth exploring. 

It also seems that there are opinions that: large-scale AI-formulations are useful in the following two other ways (hype aside). Firstly, they are useful in demonstrating the capabilities of AI work-flows and models  in this area and allow observers to draw their own extrapolations to areas which may be of future use. Different people are extrapolating differently and I think personal experience and opinion guides how we are extrapolating. Secondly (echoing some of Kevin’s points and other private ones I’ve heard), in areas where the mathematics or physics is more uncertain a large AI-formalizations can provide additional information about the underlying mathematics or physics which may be useful to individuals interested in these areas.

Naturally whether or not these uses are realized depends on a number of factors, including the presentation of the material and the expertise behind it.
This topic was moved here from #general > Learning from large-scale AI formalisations by Patrick Massot.

Kevin Buzzard said:

Example: an AI formalization today of the proof of the classification of finite simple groups would definitely be of value, because the length of the proof (14 volumes) and the fact that it is still not properly published (although it will be soon, hopefully) have raised doubts in people's minds in the community about the correctness of the result, and a huge number of other results in finite group theory and beyond rest on this important classification theorem.

While it's not relevant to your main point, I figured that I would mention that about a year ago, I asked Ron Solomon for an estimated completion date. His bottom line was, " Given that there are 26 sporadic simple groups, it would be numerologically satisfying if our work could be completed in 13 volumes and in the year ’26.  We shall see." The figure of "13 volumes" does not count Aschbacher-Smith or the rather substantial list of background results, but the main point is that 10 of those 13 volumes have been published, and 2 of the remaining three have been mostly completed (by Gernot Stroth). The remaining volume "has been the most challenging for us, as we attempt to extend two difficult papers of Michael Aschbacher under somewhat weaker hypotheses" but has apparently been going pretty well.

Until all 13 volumes are publicly available, I don't expect an AI formalization to be possible, but if anyone is seriously interested, the starting point IMO would be to formalize the background results. How hard would it be to port Feit-Thompson from Rocq to Lean?

Timothy Chow said:

if anyone is seriously interested

I am! (but not with AI)

Timothy Chow said:

How hard would it be to port Feit-Thompson from Rocq to Lean?

I'd imagine a one-to-one translation would be pretty easy for an LLM (Rocq repo link), but I'd be against this unless someone is actually working on a much larger goal (e.g. the classification) and just needs it to exist right now. I'd much rather port it by-hand and into Mathlib, to get the benefits that Kevin mentioned.

Have there been efforts for formalizing just the statement of the Classifications of finite Simple Groups? I think with (some) human scaffolding it might be a good (future) target for AI Autoformalization, but it might take a while to even formalize just the statement.

Franz Huschenbeth said:

Have there been efforts for formalizing just the statement of the Classifications of finite Simple Groups? I think with (some) human scaffolding it might be a good (future) target for AI Autoformalization, but it might take a while to even formalize just the statement.

"Just the statement" is a surprisingly loaded term here. For example, what is the formal theorem going to say about the Monster/Friendly Giant? Just that there exists a finite simple group of that order? At some point, one is going to want to prove that the group exists, and for that, one is going to want to say a lot more about the group than its order. Alternatively, one could take an even more minimalist approach, and just say that there are 26 sporadic groups, without listing them or even giving their orders. That feels inadequate somehow, but it's still a classification theorem in some sense. (Even stating that there are 26 sporadic groups requires stating what the finite groups of Lie type are, and similar issues arise there; how much are you going to say about them?)

I'm not saying that formalizing "just the statement" can't be done, but that for it to be useful, probably one needs to have some sort of game plan for the proof first, for the formalization of "just the statement" to be useful.
There's a formalization of the statement in the FormalAbstract repo. It is in Lean 3. Hasn't been done in Lean 4 I think. But it's definitely doable.
@Kevin Buzzard I hadn't though of that. I think an AI formalization today of Mochizuki's proof of the ABC conjecture would be fascinating

David Loeffler said:

Is "isolating a problem" – not just failing to prove something, but identifying a specific obstacle to why it doesn't work – something that current AI's are capable of doing? I gather some AI's automatically try to disprove as well as prove the given goal, and are very good at detecting minor misformalisations in statements in the process (starting sums at 0 instead of 1, that sort of thing); but if the AI can't find either a proof or a counterexample, can it give you a coherent account of where it got stuck, other than "I couldn't prove this lemma"? This is something that's also hard for humans!

Even if the "final" theorem is likely true (and so you can't find a counterexample), we could find that Lemma 3.7.1 is false because of some counterexample. If this happened with, say, trying to prove the ABC conjecture, then I would imagine -- assuming everyone is interested in participating and contributing to the effort in good faith -- this leads to one of three things happening:

  • Ah, this lemma has a misformalization; fix the typo and resume progress (would probably happen many times along the way).
  • This lemma, and the corresponding natural language text, neglects to mention a needed hypothesis. "Ah, you see in Chapter 3, I made it apparent I would only be considering Xs with property Y, so of course I assume that the X in this lemma satisfies that condition, which your counterexample didn't." This is much the same kind of place where humans might get stuck and confused reading a proof. That improves everyone's understanding and it moves forward.
  • There's a genuine flaw in the proof, now at a focused/minimized point, which might mean the proof falls apart (at least until someone can repair it).

That's what I would expect!
And given that AIs seem to be increasingly good at constructing counterexamples do different mistakes/misformalizations, I think this is quite workable...

But how would you check that it translated all definitions correctly. How can you check that the proof failed because of a misformalization of a definition or because of a misformalization of a proof or (which I suppose is the consensus in the mathematical community) that a proof contains a logical error, that is not easily fixable. Or it compiles correctly... (in comparator)
@Franz Huschenbeth yea, I don't know how to do that. I suppose discoveries would be made along the way. I think it is a very interesting goal though

Franz Huschenbeth said:

I do agree, but I also think that probably Mochizuki and his school would need to provide the definitions and general outline.

Definitely. The Mochizuki situation is a special case because of the massive controversy. Whenever someone insists they have a proof but the majority of experts scrutinize it and declare that there is a huge gap, generally the only way out of the impasse is for the person who claims to have a proof to spearhead the formalization. There's scant chance that a "random" person will fill the gap if the experts can't, and if "random" people fail to formalize the result then nothing has been accomplished, and the impasse remains.
